description: Explore brand guidelines from famous brands and my own client projects, with visual examples, digital portals and practical lessons for your business.
body:
Good brand guidelines make the next decision easier: which logo to use, which colors belong together, how the writing should sound, and where to find the right files.

I have collected 26 examples from well-known brands and five portals I designed for my own clients, with visual previews and practical lessons you can use when commissioning your own guidelines.

Some resources are full identity systems, some are limited logo or partner instructions, and a few are earlier examples retained for their useful structure.

I label those differences because a public logo download page is not the same deliverable as a complete brand system.

Start with the comparison below, browse the famous-brand examples, or jump to my client portals on guidelines.online.

Which kind of brand guidelines does your business need?

The right scope depends on who uses your brand and the work they need to produce.

ResourceUseful whenExamples to studyWhat to commission
Logo and partner resourcesOutside teams need the correct mark and permission rules.Asana, Netflix, MicrosoftApproved logo files, spacing, backgrounds, minimum sizes and usage terms.
Visual and verbal brand systemSeveral people create campaigns, presentations and customer communications.GitHub, Mozilla, MailchimpTypography, color roles, imagery, writing examples and templates.
Digital product guidanceA developer needs to represent your brand inside a product or integration.Spotify, GitHubInterface behavior and product examples alongside identity rules.
Client handoff portalYour team needs one place to find approved assets and specifications.Orbio, Next Dimension, Fox BermanA maintained guide with clear downloads, practical examples and an owner.

A small company does not need to copy every page of an enterprise manual.

It needs enough guidance for its real applications, whether that means a pitch deck, packaging, a website or weekly social posts.

Whether you're designing, printing, or fabricating elements of your brand identity system, everything depends on well-documented brand standards.

A brand style guide is the single most important tool for maintaining a consistent and professional brand image across all touchpoints.

The purpose of brand guidelines is simple: save time, reduce costs, and eliminate frustration by empowering your team to create a cohesive brand experience every time.

PS: Don't miss my comprehensive guide on building your digital style guide with the top 10 platforms available in 2026.

The scope of your brand guidelines will vary based on your organization's size and complexity. That's why this list includes everything from enterprise-level comprehensive guides to minimal startup-friendly examples.

What is a brand guideline?

Whether you call them brand guidelines, style guides, brand books, or brand manuals: they all serve the same purpose:

A brand guideline is a rulebook that defines how to create on-brand materials consistently.

Essentially, it's a comprehensive document outlining how to use your brand's visual and verbal assets to maintain consistency across every medium: from digital to print.

The goal is to guide designers, marketers, developers, and anyone working with your brand to produce cohesive, professional results.

What elements should brand guidelines include?

Brand guidelines come in many formats and levels of detail.

While many are distributed as PDF documents, this article compares online brand guidelines and selected downloadable references.

The online versions are often called brand portals or brand centers.

Some brand portals are extensive multi-page resources covering every brand element in granular detail.

Others focus on the essentials:

  • Logo versions and usage rules
  • Color palette specifications
  • Typography system
  • Layout and grid guidelines
  • Imagery and photography direction

Your brand guidelines can encompass both visual identity elements and verbal identity components.

This includes strategic elements like brand mission, vision statement, brand values, and tone of voice.

Want to learn how to create your own style guide? Watch my YouTube tutorial.

The examples below show different scopes of documentation; an earlier screenshot is a reference, not a promise that its original portal is still available.

26 famous-brand guideline examples

1. OpenAI

OpenAI’s public design guidelines connect visual identity, product naming and partner usage rules.

Current resource: third-party design and trademark guidance. The current page also covers typography and brand partnerships, so I use it to show how naming, visual rules and permissions work together.

They maintain a dedicated brand resource page where you can download logos and learn proper usage guidelines.

OpenAI Brand Guidelines

Alongside the visual examples, OpenAI documents naming conventions and terminology usage for people referring to its products.

The guidelines cover all the fundamentals: logo versions, usage do's and don'ts, spacing requirements, and sizing specifications.

However, their guidelines are notably rigorous about model naming, trademark compliance, and content attribution requirements.

What I would borrow: Document product names and approval rules alongside the logo so partners do not invent their own version of your brand.

2. Starbucks

Starbucks called this earlier resource the Brand Expression Guide: a comprehensive overview of how the Starbucks brand comes to life across touchpoints.

Earlier example: Starbucks Creative Expression. The screenshot and six-element breakdown below document the earlier guide; its original domain could not be securely verified during this update, so the link now opens Starbucks’ official brand-asset page.

Starbucks brand guideline

The opening sections showcase brand expressions: essentially case studies demonstrating real-world applications.

The earlier Starbucks guidelines cover six core brand elements:

  • Logo: Siren logo and logotype usage rules
  • Color: Primary green and complementary palette
  • Voice: Functional and expressive copywriting guidance
  • Typography: Headline, body, and accent font specifications
  • Illustration: Texture, collage, and graphic element usage
  • Photography: Artful, editorial, and intentional style direction

This brand microsite exemplifies excellent online brand documentation. The intuitive navigation and comprehensive coverage make it a gold standard for ensuring brand consistency.

View the current official Starbucks brand assets

What I would borrow: Show both the fixed identity elements and the range of expression a campaign is allowed to explore.

3. Dropbox

Dropbox called its earlier guidelines Design Standards: an end-to-end design system for creating clear, simple user experiences.

Current portal, with an earlier Design Standards screenshot. Dropbox now presents its public guidelines at brand.dropbox.com, with framework, voice, logo, typography, iconography, color, imagery and motion sections; the older four-part organization below remains a useful historical reference.

Dropbox brand guideline

Those standards were organized into four main sections:

  • Strategy
  • Foundation
  • Systems
  • Writing

This comprehensive style guide covers all essential brand elements and more.

Dropbox previously maintained the Design Standards site; its current public resource is the Dropbox Brand Guidelines.

Under Foundation, you'll find core elements including:

  • Logo specifications
  • Typography system
  • Color palette
  • Layout grids
  • Imagery guidelines

Unique sections like Customer Journey and Product Visuals help teams design assets quickly while maintaining consistency.

What I would borrow: Connect the visual system to the writing and the real customer journey, not just a sheet of colors.

4. Audi

Audi redesigned their corporate identity with a digital-first approach: explore their Brand Appearance guide.

Earlier example: Audi Brand Appearance. The former deep link no longer resolves; Audi’s official image page links to its CI portal, while the screenshot and scope analysis below preserve the earlier example.

Audi brand guidelines

This is arguably the most comprehensive brand guideline on this list.

Audi's guidelines cover 9 core elements:

  • Rings (logo)
  • Tagline
  • Colors
  • Typography
  • Layout Structure
  • Imagery
  • Illustration
  • Icons
  • Animation

Beyond the basics, you'll discover sections on user interface design, communication media, corporate sound, motion graphics, and more.

The guide features abundant examples and clear instructions that convey brand essentials while inspiring creative applications.

Audi's philosophy: "the brand is not a static structure but a living interface."

It's an exceptionally clear and detailed approach to brand documentation: you'll understand the Audi brand immediately.

View the current official Audi media resource

What I would borrow: Include motion and sound when those channels are part of how customers recognize your business.

5. Spotify

Spotify's Design Guidelines are uniquely focused on creating content for the Spotify ecosystem.

Specialist resource: Spotify developer design guidance. This is guidance for integrations, not a complete public manual for every Spotify marketing application.

Spotify brand guidelines

Spotify's guidelines ensure every user receives the same exceptional experience, consistently.

The guide primarily addresses content presentation within the app: album artwork, metadata display, and visual hierarchy.

It also covers browsing experiences and Spotify linking: including playing view designs and app-specific UI elements.

Core brand elements are also documented:

  • Logo usage
  • Color specifications
  • Naming restrictions
  • Typography rules

Unlike broader brand guidelines, Spotify's guide is highly specific to their platform features: with thorough explanations and well-considered details.

What I would borrow: Give developers examples that match the integration they are actually building.

6. Walmart

Walmart's brand documentation is housed in their Brand Center.

Current portal, with an earlier Brand Center screenshot. The current Walmart Brand Center covers the Spark, wordmark, color, typography, layout, Brand OS and lockups; the three-guide structure below describes the earlier resource, not the current menu.

Walmart brand guidelines

Walmart's standards contain three comprehensive guides:

  1. Accessibility conformance guide
  2. Communications brand guide
  3. Creative marketing brand guide

This robust documentation includes strategic elements like brand mission, strategic initiatives, and organizational values.

The guide goes above and beyond with specialized sections:

  • Film production guidelines
  • Vendor-tagged advertising
  • Editorial standards
  • Sub-brand management
  • And much more

Walmart’s earlier style guide was built using LingoApp: a platform for hosting brand guidelines online.

What I would borrow: Make the current assets easy to identify when the company refreshes its identity.

7. Zendesk

Zendesk previously named its guide Brandland: and it's one of the most advanced brand portals available.

Earlier example: Zendesk Brandland. The original public Brandland address now redirects to a closed help center; I retain its screenshot and scope analysis as an archive example rather than send you to that dead destination.

Zendesk Brand Guideline

Zendesk's style guide extends far beyond traditional brand identity documentation.

It includes guidance on copywriting, film production, animation, sound design, photography, and even interior design.

These guidelines ensure all writing, visual design, videos, and experiences work together to deliver a unified brand message.

Opening sections cover brand attributes and messaging framework.

The design section includes standard elements:

  • Brand identity
  • Typography
  • Color
  • Layout

Additional specialized sections include:

  • Presentation design
  • Copywriting guidelines
  • Film production
  • Brand experience

Each section contains detailed subsections, making this one of the most thorough brand documentation systems available.

What I would borrow: Scope the guide around the channels your team genuinely produces, then make those sections easy to find.

8. Keap

Keap (formerly Infusionsoft) provided an example of mid-sized company brand guidelines.

Earlier example: Keap’s public portal. The original Frontify link no longer resolves, so the screenshot below is an archive example rather than an available public download portal.

Keap brand guideline

While not as large as enterprise brands on this list, Keap demonstrates how a professional style guide should be structured.

Beyond visual basics, there's a comprehensive section on brand voice and verbal identity.

A standout feature in that earlier portal: click any logo to download assets instantly: no login or request process required.

What I would borrow: Put the correct files next to their instructions so someone can act without another email.

9. Asana

Asana's Brand Guidelines take a minimalist approach: a clean one-pager covering the essentials.

Asana brand guideline

You'll find information on logo specifications, clear space requirements, and color variations.

The Logo Don'ts section clearly illustrates common mistakes to avoid.

Additional trademark usage information is also provided.

This exemplifies a simple, effective brand guideline covering only the necessities.

What I would borrow: A short guide can be useful if it answers the most common logo and permission questions clearly.

10. Netflix

Netflix's Brand Site functions primarily as logo guidelines: keeping things deliberately minimal.

Netflix brand guidelines

Netflix guidelines cover three essential elements:

  • Logo
  • Symbol (N icon)
  • Colors

You'll also find usage restrictions and proper application examples.

The Readability section addresses contrast requirements between logo and background.

Co-branding guidance for partner logo usage is also included.

This represents one of the most streamlined approaches to online brand guidelines.

What I would borrow: Explain when to use the full wordmark and when a compact symbol is appropriate.

11. Instagram

Instagram's Brand Assets and Guidelines provide another excellent minimal guideline example.

The Instagram Brand Assets and Guidelines page contains usage instructions and legal information.

The Brand Elements section links to Instagram icon specifications and guidelines.

Here you'll find logo (glyph) usage rules with clear do's and don'ts.

Additional sections include screenshot templates and broadcast templates.

Instagram's style guide is platform-specific but straightforward: covering only the essential basics.

You'll find: logo usage, glyph specifications (black/white versions), and template downloads.

What I would borrow: Keep the latest platform-specific instructions close to the asset download.

12. TikTok

TikTok's style guide offers more depth than Instagram's minimalist approach.

TikTok brand guideline

Introductory pages describe the brand story, design concept, and underlying philosophy.

Core elements covered include:

  • Logo
  • Co-branding
  • Color
  • Typography

Overall, it's a focused style guide with everything needed to bring the TikTok brand to life consistently.

What I would borrow: Document partner lockups before an event sponsor or collaborator creates one independently.

13. ActiveCampaign

ActiveCampaign provides another example of minimal, effective brand documentation.

Current resource, with an earlier logo-page screenshot. ActiveCampaign’s current Brand Design page is substantially broader, covering color, typography, iconography, patterns, illustration, photography and voice, with a link to full guidelines in Figma.

ActiveCampaign brand guideline

The earlier page focused on essential logo usage information.

That earlier reference showed two logo color variations:

White logo: for dark backgrounds.

Base color logo (blue): for light backgrounds.

What I would borrow: Review the guide when the business adds channels; an old logo-only sheet may no longer be enough.

14. Discord

Discord's Branding Guidelines keep things simple and accessible.

Discord brand guideline

Discord's style guide is a single page covering brand basics:

  • Primary logo
  • Alternate logos
  • Spacing requirements
  • Color specifications

This represents a minimal online style guide approach.

A downloadable PDF version with additional details is also available.

For more PDF examples, see my article featuring 100 Style Guides.

What I would borrow: Offer a quick online reference as well as a downloadable document when different collaborators need both.

15. Salesforce

Salesforce houses their documentation in Brand Central.

Salesforce brand guideline

The site covers brand values and strategic elements alongside visual guidelines:

  • Logo
  • Color
  • Typography

Salesforce's guidelines function as a style guide within a style guide: each element has a dedicated sub-page with comprehensive details.

Exploring all pages reveals more depth than the surface suggests.

What I would borrow: Organize the guide around specific tasks so a marketer can find a rule without reading everything.

16. YouTube

YouTube's guidelines are called Brand Resources.

YouTube brand guidelines

YouTube's brand resources cover four essential elements:

  • Logo
  • Icon
  • Colors
  • Do's & Don'ts

You'll find logo usage rules, minimum sizes, placement guidelines, color versions, and application examples.

YouTube's style guide is concise yet complete: everything essential in one place.

This exemplifies the most basic approach to creating an effective online style guide.

What I would borrow: Use examples to remove ambiguity about small sizes and difficult backgrounds.

17. IBM

IBM's guidelines are titled IBM Logo and Brand Guidelines for Third Parties.

Specialist resource: third-party logo and brand rules. The linked IBM PDF is intended for third parties; do not mistake that scope for IBM’s entire internal identity or product design system.

IBM brand guidelines

IBM's comprehensive guidelines include 13 sections covering:

  • Logo Usage
  • Colors
  • Trademark Licensing
  • Context
  • Restrictions
  • Merchandise
  • Review Process

IBM maintains strict trademark and logo usage rules to protect brand integrity: usage requires a trademark license agreement.

The language is direct, formal, and authoritative: matching IBM's professional brand personality.

Visual examples demonstrate proper and improper usage clearly.

Clear hierarchy and logical structure prioritize licensing and context before visual rules.

The tone balances helpfulness with firmness: educating third parties while enforcing compliance.

Specific language like "you must" and "don't" indicates clear mandates.

Violations are illustrated with explanations, reinforcing adherence importance.

The writing is concise and precise: matching IBM's brand character.

What I would borrow: Distinguish how an asset should look from whether someone has permission to use it.

18. LG

LG's Branding Guidelines take a more casual, approachable tone.

Current identity overview, with an earlier guideline screenshot. I have replaced the unofficial PDF mirror with LG’s own identity site, which covers logo, color and gradients, photography, typography, slogan, voice and design system.

LG Branding Guidelines

The earlier LG guidelines are more conversational: matching their approachable, lifestyle brand positioning.

Elements covered include:

  • LG Logo
  • Colors
  • Co-Branding
  • Promotional Items and Apparel
  • Advertising
  • Approval Process

Plain language explains concepts clearly: focusing on understanding over strict compliance.

While rules exist, language like "preferred" allows some flexibility.

Visual examples take precedence over dense text: simple iconography demonstrates proper usage.

Logical structure progresses from logo to color to co-branding to merchandising to approval.

Less emphasis on legal compliance compared to IBM: the tone offers guidance aligned with brand values rather than strict demands.

Soft language like "Please avoid..." creates a collaborative, educational feel.

View the current official LG identity overview

What I would borrow: Explain the intended personality through real applications as well as written rules.

19. Freepik

Freepik's guidelines build a distinctive, creative brand identity focused on inspiration and empowerment.

Earlier example: Freepik’s brand guide. The former Freepik design address now redirects to Magnific’s official press resources; the screenshot and language analysis below describe the earlier Freepik guide, not the current Magnific identity.

Freepik branding guidelines

The conversational, friendly tone uses words like "let's" and "we": creating an inclusive atmosphere.

Clear explanations provide rationale behind brand decisions, not just rules.

Elements covered:

  • Who we are
  • Why we exist
  • Our Assets
  • Logo
  • Isotype
  • Color
  • Typography

Language aims to inspire creativity with words like "joyful", "rebelliousness", and "kaleidoscopic."

Flexibility encourages creative expression: "preferred" rather than absolute mandates.

Narrative elements explain Freepik's story and mission: beyond dry rules.

Whimsical touches reinforce brand personality throughout.

The peer-to-peer guidance tone creates collaborative energy.

Freepik's guidelines use approachable language and narrative to educate, inspire, and build inclusivity: inviting partners to co-create the brand story.

View the current official Magnific press resource

What I would borrow: Use the writing in the guide to demonstrate the brand’s voice, then keep the source current as the brand evolves.

20. GitHub

GitHub’s Brand Toolkit brings identity, writing, graphic elements, applications and motion into one navigable resource.

Its sections include accessibility, color, logo, typography, diagrams, illustration, mascots and product UI, alongside presentations, social, web and event examples.

I like the separation between brand foundations and work in use, because a color value alone does not tell someone how to build a slide or explain a product.

The toolkit also links to Primer resources, making the relationship between the brand and interface systems easier to explore.

What I would borrow: give a growing software company a small set of approved applications, not just a visual vocabulary.

Start with the templates your sales, marketing and product teams use most often, then expand the library when the work demands it.

Explore GitHub’s official resource

21. NASA

NASA’s Graphic Standards show how a recognizable identity needs clear rules when many teams and outside organizations encounter it.

The current resource distinguishes the NASA insignia, logotype and supporting identifiers, with guidance on typography and additional restrictions.

It also distinguishes print recommendations from the fonts used by its digital Horizon Design System.

This is useful because a logo family can become confusing when different marks have different roles.

What I would borrow: name the primary mark, explain the role of secondary marks, and show which combinations are appropriate.

Keep the question of permission separate from the visual specification; an available reference image is not blanket permission to use another organization’s identity.

Explore NASA’s official resource

22. Slack

Slack’s Media Kit is a practical entry point for someone who needs an official logo or product screenshot quickly.

It separates logo assets from screenshots and points toward a broader Brand Center for deeper guidance.

The public kit describes screenshots for desktop, mobile and tablet, which is a useful reminder that brand handoff can include product materials as well as identity files.

I would treat this page as a media and partner resource, rather than assume that its public surface contains the entire Slack identity system.

What I would borrow: create a short route to the assets people request repeatedly, with deeper rules available separately.

If the wider guide changes location, keep this entry page and its outbound links maintained so the fastest path does not become a dead end.

Explore Slack’s official resource

23. Mailchimp

Mailchimp is especially useful because its visual assets and content style guide answer different parts of the same brand problem.

The brand-assets page gives partners a reference for using the identity, while the voice-and-tone guide explains how writing changes with the reader’s situation.

The distinction is practical: the underlying voice can stay recognizable while a support message adopts a different tone from a celebration.

For a founder, this matters when the person writing sales emails is different from the person creating the website.

What I would borrow: include a few realistic examples of product copy, customer support and social captions alongside the logo rules.

Describe the decision behind each example so a writer can apply the principle to a new situation.

Explore Mailchimp’s official resource

24. Mozilla

Mozilla’s Brand Guidelines connect the organization’s mission with voice, messaging and visual elements.

The public navigation separates those guideline sections from logo, mascot, icon, illustration, press and editorial libraries.

Its wider portal also distinguishes the Mozilla, Mozilla Foundation and Firefox brands instead of treating every mark as interchangeable.

That is a useful model for a company with several products or organizational identities.

What I would borrow: explain which brand someone should use before asking them to choose a file.

A clearly named library and a short starting section can make a large portal more approachable for someone who only visits it occasionally.

Explore Mozilla’s official resource

25. Microsoft

Microsoft’s Trademark and Brand Guidelines demonstrate the permission side of documenting a large brand.

The page addresses names, logos, product icons and other brand assets, and explains that many uses require authorization.

It uses a fictional partner to illustrate situations where someone refers to Microsoft products without suggesting an endorsement.

This is third-party usage guidance, not an open replacement for Microsoft’s full internal creative system.

What I would borrow: make partnership and co-branding rules explicit when distributors, resellers or technology partners use your name.

Show what relationship a badge or lockup communicates, who approves it, and where collaborators should go when the standard example does not fit.

Explore Microsoft’s official resource

26. Reddit

Reddit’s brand page introduces the logo, Snoo and Reddit Sans before directing visitors to specialized resource collections.

Those collections cover guidelines, logo assets, typography, traits and values, and the mascot.

The overview explains how the conversational identity and the readable type system relate to the community the brand serves.

I find this useful as a model for giving a distinctive character a clear role, rather than letting a mascot become an unrelated decoration.

What I would borrow: introduce the central idea first, then let a visitor choose the specific resource they need.

If your brand includes a mascot, define its personality and role alongside the files, and make any commercial-use requirements easy to find.

Explore Reddit’s official resource

Brand guidelines I designed for my clients

I used to deliver my clients’ brand guidelines as landscape PDF presentations.

That format is still useful for reviewing a complete identity or keeping a dated record of what was approved.

But in my client workflow, those PDFs could get lost in email, and finding the right logo often meant returning to a separate folder.

I created guidelines.online to put the guide and the working assets into a digital portal I use with my clients.

The aim is straightforward: one link to the identity rules, color specifications, typography and approved assets.

That gives my clients a practical place to return to after the identity presentation.

A portal still needs someone to keep it current, and a PDF can remain useful alongside it.

27. Orbio

For Orbio, I built the guidelines around a distinctive orb and an editorial visual system for an AI business.

The portal brings primary and stacked logo arrangements together with the standalone mark, light and dark versions, color specifications and typography.

The palette includes Void, Marble, Stone, Brass and a Vein orange accent, so the guide needs to make those choices reproducible beyond the original presentation.

I also wanted the identity to connect to practical applications, rather than stop at the logo page.

The handoff lesson: explain which asset fits a given space and keep the supporting files close to the rules.

28. Next Dimension

For Next Dimension, I designed an identity that gives a healthcare AI company a more distinctive visual character.

The portal documents horizontal and vertical logo arrangements, the standalone mark and examples of incorrect use.

Its Deep Space and Violet Dream colors sit alongside a wider supporting palette, with separate typography roles.

Putting those specifications in the same place makes the relationship between the presentation and the implementation easier to follow.

The handoff lesson: document the variations that a website, presentation or printed item will actually need, rather than making the team improvise them.

View Next Dimension’s brand guidelines · Explore the project

29. Savory

Savory is my newest real-estate identity project, and this portal shows how I am organizing its guidelines and assets.

The guide brings the wordmark, stamp, compact favicon and team lockups into one place, with color and typography specifications.

Wax Red, Sky Blue and the supporting neutrals connect those variations into one recognizable system.

The applications section provides context for using the identity across touchpoints, rather than treating each version as an unrelated logo.

The handoff lesson: give the team a clear choice between the full name, the supporting seal and the smallest digital mark.

The portal is a view of the identity system, not a claim that the client’s wider website or rollout is complete.

View Savory’s brand guidelines · Explore the project

30. Fox Berman

For Fox Berman, the guidelines organize a law firm’s identity into primary and stacked logos plus a compact monogram.

The portal pairs those files with the Dark Grey, Cream and Tropical color specifications and the typography reference.

Those variations matter when the same identity needs to appear in a narrow header, a presentation or a smaller social placement.

The handoff lesson: name the files by their role and show the intended background, so the team does not have to guess from a folder of similar exports.

View Fox Berman’s brand guidelines · Explore the project

31. Elevate AB

For Elevate AB, the portal separates the logo, mark and wordmark and documents the supporting color and type system.

Blue, Green and Lavender sit alongside Black and White, with primary and secondary typography roles.

This is the kind of practical reference a small software team can use without navigating a large enterprise manual.

The handoff lesson: a focused guide should make the everyday decisions easy first, then grow as the brand adds more applications.

View Elevate AB’s brand guidelines · Explore the project

What to ask for when commissioning brand guidelines

A useful guide should answer the questions your team faces after the identity presentation is over.

1. Agree on the actual applications

List the materials you need to create in the next few months before deciding how extensive the documentation should be.

A sales-led business may need presentation and proposal examples, while a retailer may need packaging and signage rules.

Commission the decisions and examples that support that work, not an arbitrary page count.

2. Specify the logo files and their roles

Ask for vector masters and useful screen exports, together with an explanation of when to use each lockup.

The guide should cover spacing, small sizes, approved backgrounds and mistakes to avoid.

A folder containing twenty unnamed variations is not a clear handoff.

3. Document color and type for real production

Separate screen values from print specifications, and make the role of each color clear.

Typography needs an explanation of hierarchy and usage, not just the name of a typeface.

Confirm which font licenses your team and outside suppliers need before they use or distribute font files.

4. Include examples of the writing and imagery

Show a headline, a short product description or a customer message so the intended voice becomes concrete.

For photography and illustration, explain what belongs in the system and what would feel out of place.

Examples turn preferences into decisions that another person can repeat.

5. Plan for access, approvals and maintenance

Choose who owns the guide, who can update it, and how the team will recognize the current approved version.

A public page is useful for public assets, while unreleased work or internal documents may need controlled access.

Ask what happens when a logo file changes or a new campaign template is added.

Make those responsibilities part of the scope before the handoff, rather than an assumption afterward.

PDF or digital brand portal?

I choose the format around how the client will use the guidelines.

A PDF is useful for a presentation, offline reference, print review or an approval snapshot.

A digital portal is useful when people need a shared place to find instructions and download the current assets.

The portal does not remove the need for clear rules, sensible access settings or regular maintenance.

For my own client work, guidelines.online brings those everyday references together, while a presentation can still explain the thinking behind the identity.

Questions business owners ask about brand guidelines

How detailed should our brand guidelines be?

Detailed enough that someone outside the original design process can create your most common materials without guessing.

Start with the core identity and a few real applications, then add specialist guidance when the business needs it.

Are brand guidelines the same as a design system?

They overlap, but a brand guide explains identity and expression, while a product design system can go further into interface components, states, behavior and implementation.

Spotify and GitHub are useful references for seeing where those needs connect.

Can we copy a famous brand’s guidelines?

Study the structure and clarity, then build rules around your own identity, audience and applications.

The examples here are references, not permission to reuse another brand’s logos, typography or creative assets.

What should we receive from a designer?

Agree on the identity assets, documentation, practical examples, licensing responsibilities and handoff format before starting.

My logo design cost guide explains why comparing scope matters more than comparing a headline price.
